confidence.rationale: Convergent reviews distinguish multiple observational effects, but terminology and mechanism classification remain contested.

limitations: The definition does not imply that all social-learning effects share one cognitive or neural mechanism.

scope.population: Human and nonhuman observers represented in the cited reviews.
scope.temporal_scope: Observation and later behavior under declared tests.

claims.statement: Social learning can change attention, expectations, acquired responses, or performance after observing others; exact imitation is only one possible outcome and mechanism.

causal_assumptions.consistency: Children received the scripted aggressive, nonaggressive, or no-model condition represented by their group.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Matching on baseline aggression and sex reduced some imbalance; unmeasured imbalance and historical assignment procedures remain possible.
causal_assumptions.interference: Behavior of one tested child is assumed not to alter another child's assigned exposure or test response.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Children were represented across aggressive, nonaggressive, and no-model conditions.

claims.causal_estimand: Difference in immediate protocol-coded imitative aggression between aggressive-model exposure and the declared comparison conditions.

confidence.rationale: The modeled behavior was experimentally controlled and comparison groups were matched, but the small historical sample and immediate artificial test sharply limit generalization.

limitations: The experiment establishes an immediate task effect, not durable aggression, real-world transfer, or one unique learning mechanism.

boundary_conditions: Live adult aggressive-model exposure, Bobo-doll materials, historical nursery-school sample, and immediate coded behavior.
scope.population: 72 children aged 37 to 69 months from one Stanford University nursery school.
scope.temporal_scope: Immediate play test after model exposure and standardized frustration induction.

claims.statement: In the 1961 nursery-school experiment, assignment to observe an aggressive adult model increased later protocol-coded imitative aggression relative to nonaggressive-model and no-model conditions.
claims.temporal_ordering: Model exposure preceded the frustration procedure and later behavior observation.

causal_assumptions.consistency: The three films differed in the declared consequence ending while retaining the modeled response sequence.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Experimental assignment supports comparison, but the source's small sample and matching procedures leave residual uncertainty.
causal_assumptions.interference: Cross-child interference is assumed absent during individual testing.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Participants were represented in all three model-consequence conditions.

claims.causal_estimand: Difference in spontaneous matching responses across assigned model-rewarded, model-punished, and no-consequence conditions.

confidence.rationale: The model consequence was experimentally manipulated and the immediate performance contrast was clear, but the sample was small and restricted to one aggressive film and setting.

limitations: The observed consequence changed immediate performance and does not by itself show different acquisition of the modeled repertoire.

boundary_conditions: Film-mediated aggressive model, rewarded, punished, or no-consequence ending, and immediate matching-response test.
scope.population: 66 children aged approximately 3 to 5 years from one nursery school.
scope.temporal_scope: Spontaneous reproduction test immediately after the modeled consequence film.

claims.statement: In Bandura's 1965 experiment, the consequence shown for an aggressive model changed children's spontaneous matching responses, with fewer responses after observed punishment than after reward or no consequence.
claims.temporal_ordering: The observed model consequence preceded spontaneous observer performance testing.

causal_assumptions.consistency: Children received the declared incentive for reproducing modeled responses.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Each prior condition was tested under the incentive phase; order and carryover from spontaneous testing may affect interpretation.
causal_assumptions.interference: Cross-child interference is assumed absent during testing.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Children from every prior model-consequence condition received the incentive opportunity.

claims.causal_estimand: Within-study change in modeled-response reproduction after direct observer incentives and the remaining difference between prior model-consequence groups.

confidence.rationale: The within-study incentive phase directly tested available reproduction, while interpretation as equivalent acquisition depends on the validity and ceiling properties of that probe.

limitations: Equal incentive-assisted responding supports an acquisition-performance distinction but does not prove identical memory, attention, or durable learning across groups.

boundary_conditions: Direct reward for reproducing the same modeled aggressive responses after initial spontaneous testing.
scope.population: The same 66 children represented in the 1965 model-consequence experiment.
scope.temporal_scope: Incentive-assisted reproduction after the spontaneous imitation test.

claims.statement: In the later incentive test of Bandura's 1965 experiment, offering children direct rewards for reproducing modeled responses increased performance and removed the earlier differences between model-consequence groups.
claims.temporal_ordering: The direct reproduction incentive was introduced after model exposure and spontaneous performance testing.

confidence.rationale: The acquisition-performance dissociation constrains explanations, but the cited studies do not uniquely identify attention, representation, associative learning, motivation, or motor reproduction as the mechanism.

claims.falsifiable_boundary: The hypothesis is weakened when observer incentives and opportunity do not reveal retained modeled information or when nonobservational controls explain the response equally well.
limitations: The hypothesis is not a validated universal four-stage sequence and should not be used to infer an unmeasured internal representation from imitation alone.

boundary_conditions: Declared model exposure, distinct spontaneous and prompted tests, and observable matching-response criteria.
scope.temporal_scope: Observation, retention interval, and later spontaneous or prompted performance.

claims.statement: Observation may establish action-relevant information while observed consequences, direct incentives, motor capacity, and context jointly determine whether a matching response is performed.
claims.temporal_ordering: Observation precedes retention and later opportunities for spontaneous or incentivized response production.

evidence.design: Matched controlled laboratory experiment with scripted live-model exposure and immediate behavioral observation.
evidence.extraction_locator: Method, results, and summary reporting 72 children assigned to aggressive-model, nonaggressive-model, or no-model conditions.
limitations: Small single-site historical sample, artificial materials, induced frustration, immediate outcome measurement, and possible expectancy or demand effects limit generalization.
evidence.population: 36 girls and 36 boys aged 37 to 69 months from the Stanford University Nursery School.
evidence.summary: Children exposed to the aggressive model produced substantially more protocol-matching physical and verbal aggression than nonaggressive-model and control groups in the immediate test.

evidence.design: Controlled film-model experiment with three assigned consequence conditions and immediate spontaneous reproduction test.
evidence.extraction_locator: Postexposure spontaneous-performance test comparing model rewarded, punished, and no-consequence conditions.
limitations: The result concerns immediate aggressive-response performance after one film and does not directly measure durable acquisition or real-world behavior.
evidence.population: 66 nursery-school children, 33 girls and 33 boys, aged approximately 3 to 5 years.
evidence.summary: Children who observed the model punished produced fewer spontaneous matching responses than children who observed reward or no consequence.

evidence.design: Within-study incentive-assisted reproduction phase across the three prior model-consequence groups.
evidence.extraction_locator: Incentive phase following spontaneous testing, in which direct rewards were offered for reproducing modeled responses.
limitations: Incentive-assisted reproduction can be affected by motivation, motor ability, demand characteristics, memory retrieval, and ceiling effects.
evidence.population: The same 66 nursery-school children included in the model-consequence experiment.
evidence.summary: Direct incentives increased reproduction and removed the prior between-group differences, indicating that low spontaneous performance did not imply absence of available modeled responses.

evidence.design: Mechanism-oriented interpretation of experimentally separated spontaneous and incentivized reproduction tests.
evidence.extraction_locator: Comparison of spontaneous and incentive-assisted tests interpreted by the author as acquisition versus performance.
limitations: One operational acquisition probe cannot uniquely distinguish attention, retention, response availability, motivation, and demand effects.
evidence.population: 66 nursery-school children in the included experiment.
evidence.summary: The dissociation is compatible with model consequences affecting performance more than available acquisition, but it does not identify the internal process producing that difference.

evidence.design: Comparative narrative review of social-learning functions and candidate cognitive mechanisms.
evidence.extraction_locator: Review synthesis distinguishing social input mechanisms from domain-general associative learning mechanisms.
limitations: The review advances a theoretical synthesis and does not establish one universal mechanism for human observational learning.
evidence.population: Human and nonhuman social-learning studies reviewed by the author.
evidence.summary: The review argues that social and asocial learning can depend on shared associative mechanisms while social perceptual, attentional, and motivational inputs tune what is learned.

metadata.description: Separates observing a model, modeled behavior, observed consequences, acquisition, spontaneous performance, incentive-assisted reproduction, and competing social-learning mechanisms.
metadata.title: Evidence pack for social and observational learning

boundary_notes: Social learning is broader than exact imitation and can involve attention, outcome learning, emulation, instruction, or response facilitation.
A behavior observed immediately after demonstration is performance evidence, not by itself proof of durable learning or transfer.
objects.definition: Acquisition or modification of information, expectations, skills, or behavior following observation of another agent or the consequences associated with that agent's behavior.
objects.label: Observational social learning

objects.definition: Declared setting in which an observer is exposed to another agent performing a specified action or sequence before later testing.
objects.label: Modeled-behavior observation context
objects.scope: Controlled model-exposure procedures represented by the included studies.

objects.definition: Observable action or action sequence performed by a model and made available for an observer to see or hear.
objects.function_note: Demonstration does not establish what information the observer attended to or retained.
objects.label: Modeled demonstration behavior
objects.response_topography: Protocol-defined physical, verbal, or object-directed behavior performed by the model.

objects.definition: Experimental assignment to observe a model perform a declared target behavior rather than a comparison model or no model.
objects.delivery: Study-specific live or recorded modeled behavior shown before the observer test.
objects.label: Model-behavior exposure

boundary_notes: The consequence is delivered to the model, not directly contingent on the observer's behavior.
objects.definition: Experimentally assigned reward, punishment, or no-consequence event shown after the model performs the target behavior.
objects.delivery: Film-mediated model consequence presented before spontaneous observer performance testing.
objects.label: Observed consequence for the model

objects.definition: Offer of a reward contingent on the observer reproducing as many modeled responses as possible during a later test.
objects.delivery: Explicit attractive incentives offered after the spontaneous imitation test.
objects.label: Direct incentive for observer reproduction

boundary_notes: This representation is inferred from later performance and is not directly observed.
Similar reproduction can arise through different representational or associative processes.
objects.definition: Proposed retained information about the observed action that can support later description or reproduction under suitable conditions.
objects.label: Encoded representation of modeled action

objects.definition: Observable response by the observer that matches a protocol-defined feature of the demonstrated action.
objects.function_note: Topographic matching does not uniquely identify imitation, learning, identification, or motivation.
objects.label: Observer matching response
objects.response_topography: Study-coded physical, verbal, or object-directed response corresponding to the model's behavior.

objects.definition: Count or rate of matching responses emitted in the post-observation test without a new direct reproduction incentive.
objects.label: Spontaneous modeled-response frequency

objects.definition: Trained observation and coding of protocol-defined matching responses during a post-exposure performance test.
objects.label: Spontaneous imitation coding
objects.method: Code declared matching and nonmatching responses in fixed observation intervals using the study protocol.

boundary_notes: Incentive-assisted reproduction is an operational probe of acquisition, not a pure or complete measure of stored knowledge.
objects.definition: Count of modeled responses reproduced when the observer is explicitly rewarded for demonstrating what was retained.
objects.label: Incentive-assisted reproduction test
objects.method: Offer a declared reward for reproducing modeled responses and code the resulting response repertoire.

boundary_notes: The complete sequence is an integrative hypothesis and does not establish a unique social-cognitive mechanism.
Observed consequences can affect performance without being direct reinforcement of the observer's prior response.
objects.definition: Proposed process in which model exposure supports retention of action-relevant information while observed and direct consequences alter whether and when a matching response is performed.
objects.label: Observation-to-performance selection
realization_conditions: The observer has perceptual access to the modeled behavior.
Later tests distinguish spontaneous performance from incentive-assisted reproduction.
Alternative attentional, associative, motor, and motivational accounts remain testable.

sources.title: Influence of models' reinforcement contingencies on the acquisition of imitative responses

sources.authority_note: Peer-reviewed comparative review used to prevent social input from being equated with one special-purpose learning mechanism.
sources.title: What's social about social learning?

sources.authority_note: Review used for explicit distinctions among observational effects on performance, acquisition, and conditioned reinforcement.
sources.title: Observational learning
